title: Honoring guests
tomorrow: Dadi insists on carrying the heavy pot herself. do you let her?

cards: Before guests arrive, a house has a smell. Onions going soft. Cardamom cracked for coffee.
Something in the oven a little longer than planned. So what gets made first? In the Qur'an, Abraham answers without a speech.
Strangers come to his door and say peace. He says peace back, and then, before anyone has explained who they are, he slips away to his household and comes back with a fatted calf.

teach.b: The Qur'an asks it as a question, in Pickthall's words: "Hath the story of Abraham's honoured guests reached thee?" He doesn't ask for names first. He doesn't check what they're owed.
He brings the food and sets it before them himself, and says: "Will ye not eat?" The honor is in the hurry and the setting-down. The Prophet ﷺ made it part of faith.
In Sahih al-Bukhari: whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honor his guest. Another report gives it a shape: a day and a night of your best, and hospitality for up to three days.
Notice how much of it is the senses. A guest is honored through the nose, the mouth and the hands before much is said: coffee smelled at the door, a plate set down, a seat pulled out.
And here's something a Christian or Jewish neighbor would recognize.

teach.h: AN OPEN TENT IN GENESIS TOO.
teach.b: Abraham's visitors appear in the book of Genesis too, where he runs to meet strangers at his tent and hurries to bring bread and a calf. One open tent, remembered in more than one scripture.
One to tell a friend tonight: in the Qur'an, Abraham feeds his guests before he knows who they are.

how: Muslims treat hospitality as part of faith: guests are offered coffee or tea and food when they arrive, and fed before any business is discussed.

o: a party thrown for a family's important visitors
inviting only people who will invite you back
welcoming whoever comes, and feeding them well

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: a day and a night of your best
bread and a calf at a tent

s: in the Qur'an, Abraham asks his guests who they are before feeding them
they say peace, he says peace, and he goes to bring the calf.
a hadith ties honoring guests to believing in God and the Last Day
whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honor his guest.
Abraham's visitors appear in the Bible's book of Genesis too
he hurries to bring them bread and a calf.

games.q: a new kid from your class shows up at your door unannounced, right as your family sits down to eat. what fits 'honor your guest'?
o: tell him it's dinnertime and he can come back tomorrow.
pull up a chair and set a plate before asking why he came.
let him wait in the living room until everyone's done.
games.why: Abraham fed strangers before he knew who they were. the plate comes first; the reason for the visit can wait.

practice: If there's something to drink or eat near you, coffee, tea, water, a date, take one slow sip or bite as if you were the guest.
Notice the warmth or the cool, the taste, and what it would mean if someone had made it for you before asking your name. Then picture setting the same cup down in front of someone else.

wordCard.voice: Honoring guests: welcoming and feeding whoever comes to the door, before the questions. Abraham brought the calf first.

orig.note: Arabic: a guest; Qur'an 51:24 speaks of Abraham's honored guests.

carryVoice: Your line: honor guests, and let the coffee come before the questions. Eight of ten.

sources.q: Hath the story of Abraham's honoured guests reached thee

sources.ref: Qur'an 51:25–27 (they said peace; he went to his household, brought a fatted calf and set it before them)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6018–6019 (whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honor his guest; the guest's due is a day and a night; hospitality is three days)
Genesis 18:1–8 (Abraham runs to meet three men at his tent and brings bread and a calf)
